claim: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease in Western countries.
source: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease in Western countries.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but is presented as established knowledge.

claim: NAFLD has a prevalence rate of 21–25% in North American and Europe.
source: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common chronic liver disease in Western countries, with a prevalence rate of 21–25% in North American and Europe (Loomba and Sanyal, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Loomba and Sanyal, 2013.

claim: Dysbiosis of the intestinal microbiota and disruption of microbiota-host interactions contribute to the pathology of NAFLD.
source: There is growing evidence that dysbiosis of the intestinal microbiota and disruption of microbiota-host interactions contribute to the pathology of NAFLD.
evidence: This is stated as growing evidence in the abstract and introduction, implying support from the literature.

claim: Gut microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolite indole-3-acetate (I3A) was decreased in both cecum and liver of high-fat diet-fed mice.
source: We previously demonstrated that gut microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolite indole-3-acetate (I3A) was decreased in both cecum and liver of high-fat diet-fed mice
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors, supported by citation to their prior study.

claim: I3A attenuated the expression of inflammatory cytokines in macrophages.
source: We previously demonstrated that gut microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolite indole-3-acetate (I3A) was decreased in both cecum and liver of high-fat diet-fed mice and attenuated the expression of inflammatory cytokines in macrophages
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: I3A attenuated Tnfa and fatty acid-induced inflammatory responses in an aryl-hydrocarbon receptor (AhR)-dependent manner in hepatocytes.
source: We previously demonstrated that gut microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolite indole-3-acetate (I3A) was decreased in both cecum and liver of high-fat diet-fed mice and attenuated the expression of inflammatory cytokines in macrophages and Tnfa and fatty acid-induced inflammatory responses in an aryl-hydrocarbon receptor (AhR)-dependent manner in hepatocytes.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased serum ALT compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
source: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased serum ALT, hepatic triglycerides (TG), liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and hepatic production of inflammatory cytokines, compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased hepatic triglycerides (TG) compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
source: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased serum ALT, hepatic triglycerides (TG), liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and hepatic production of inflammatory cytokines, compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased liver steatosis compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
source: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased serum ALT, hepatic triglycerides (TG), liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and hepatic production of inflammatory cytokines, compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased hepatocyte ballooning compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
source: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased serum ALT, hepatic triglycerides (TG), liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and hepatic production of inflammatory cytokines, compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased lobular inflammation compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
source: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased serum ALT, hepatic triglycerides (TG), liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and hepatic production of inflammatory cytokines, compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased hepatic production of inflammatory cytokines compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
source: Western diet (WD)-fed mice given sugar water (SW) with I3A showed dramatically decreased serum ALT, hepatic triglycerides (TG), liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, lobular inflammation, and hepatic production of inflammatory cytokines, compared to WD-fed mice given only SW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: I3A administration did not significantly modify the intestinal microbiome.
source: Metagenomic analysis show that I3A administration did not significantly modify the intestinal microbiome, suggesting that I3A's beneficial effects likely reflect the metabolite's direct actions on the liver.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: I3A's beneficial effects likely reflect the metabolite's direct actions on the liver.
source: Metagenomic analysis show that I3A administration did not significantly modify the intestinal microbiome, suggesting that I3A's beneficial effects likely reflect the metabolite's direct actions on the liver.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the microbiome was not significantly altered.

claim: Administration of I3A partially reversed WD-induced alterations of liver metabolome.
source: Administration of I3A partially reversed WD-induced alterations of liver metabolome and proteome, notably, decreasing expression of several enzymes in hepatic lipogenesis and β-oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Administration of I3A partially reversed WD-induced alterations of liver proteome.
source: Administration of I3A partially reversed WD-induced alterations of liver metabolome and proteome, notably, decreasing expression of several enzymes in hepatic lipogenesis and β-oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Administration of I3A decreased expression of several enzymes in hepatic lipogenesis.
source: Administration of I3A partially reversed WD-induced alterations of liver metabolome and proteome, notably, decreasing expression of several enzymes in hepatic lipogenesis and β-oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Administration of I3A decreased expression of several enzymes in hepatic β-oxidation.
source: Administration of I3A partially reversed WD-induced alterations of liver metabolome and proteome, notably, decreasing expression of several enzymes in hepatic lipogenesis and β-oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 5.

claim: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) mediates the anti-inflammatory effects of I3A in macrophages.
source: Mechanistically, we also show that AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) mediates the anti-inflammatory effects of I3A in macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Approximately 25% of individuals having liver steatosis develop NASH.
source: Approximately 25% of individuals having liver steatosis develop NASH, which is characterized by liver inflammation, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and cell damage (Tiniakos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tiniakos et al., 2010.

claim: NASH is characterized by liver inflammation, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and cell damage.
source: Approximately 25% of individuals having liver steatosis develop NASH, which is characterized by liver inflammation, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and cell damage (Tiniakos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tiniakos et al., 2010.

claim: A subset of NASH patients develops cirrhosis and even hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: A subset of NASH patients develops cirrhosis and even hepatocellular carcinoma (Calzadilla Bertot and Adams, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Calzadilla Bertot and Adams, 2016.

claim: There are currently no pharmacological treatments available for NASH.
source: Although significant progress has been made in understanding the pathogenesis of NAFLD, factors leading to the progression from steatosis to NASH remain poorly understood, and there are currently no pharmacological treatments available for NASH.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Expansion of the phyla Verrucomicrobia and Proteobacteria correlates with NASH in both human and animal studies.
source: Certain shifts in the intestinal microbiota community composition, e.g., expansion of the phyla Verrucomicrobia and Proteobacteria, correlate with NASH in both human and animal studies (Hoyles et al., 2018; Le Roy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hoyles et al., 2018 and Le Roy et al., 2013.

claim: Compromised intestinal barrier integrity promotes the translocation of bacterial products from the lumen to circulation.
source: One potential mechanism linking intestinal microbiota dysbiosis and NASH is compromised intestinal barrier integrity, which promotes the translocation of bacterial products from the lumen to circulation.
evidence: This is stated as a potential mechanism based on existing knowledge.

claim: Translocation of bacterial products can contribute directly and indirectly (through intestinal inflammation) to liver inflammation.
source: One potential mechanism linking intestinal microbiota dysbiosis and NASH is compromised intestinal barrier integrity, which promotes the translocation of bacterial products from the lumen to circulation. This can contribute directly and indirectly (through intestinal inflammation) to liver inflammation (Saltzman et al., 2018; Bibbò et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saltzman et al., 2018; Bibbò et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2019.

claim: Microbial dysbiosis alters the balance of bioactive metabolites produced by gut bacteria such as bile acids, short chain fatty acids, and aromatic amino acid derivatives.
source: Additionally, microbial dysbiosis alters the balance of bioactive metabolites produced by gut bacteria such as bile acids, short chain fatty acids, and aromatic amino acid derivatives, which have been shown to impact liver metabolism and inflammation in NAFLD through host receptor-mediated pathways (Ding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ding et al., 2019.

claim: Bioactive metabolites produced by gut bacteria have been shown to impact liver metabolism and inflammation in NAFLD through host receptor-mediated pathways.
source: Additionally, microbial dysbiosis alters the balance of bioactive metabolites produced by gut bacteria such as bile acids, short chain fatty acids, and aromatic amino acid derivatives, which have been shown to impact liver metabolism and inflammation in NAFLD through host receptor-mediated pathways (Ding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ding et al., 2019.

claim: The levels of I3A were significantly reduced in fecal material of Western diet (WD)-fed mice compared to control mice at weeks 8 and 16.
source: Similar to our previous finding in HFD-fed mice (Krishnan et al., 2018), the levels of I3A were significantly reduced in fecal material (50% and 64% decrease at weeks 8 and 16, respectively) and the liver (70% decrease at week 16) of Western diet (WD)-fed mice compared to CN fed an LFD (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The levels of I3A were significantly reduced in the liver of Western diet (WD)-fed mice compared to control mice at week 16.
source: Similar to our previous finding in HFD-fed mice (Krishnan et al., 2018), the levels of I3A were significantly reduced in fecal material (50% and 64% decrease at weeks 8 and 16, respectively) and the liver (70% decrease at week 16) of Western diet (WD)-fed mice compared to CN fed an LFD (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice that were given WD and sugar water (SW) containing I3A showed increased I3A levels in fecal material compared to mice given the same WD and SW without I3A.
source: Mice that were given WD and sugar water (SW) containing I3A showed increased I3A levels in fecal material, the liver and serum compared to mice given the same WD and SW without I3A (Figure 1A, B, and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mice that were given WD and sugar water (SW) containing I3A showed increased I3A levels in the liver compared to mice given the same WD and SW without I3A.
source: Mice that were given WD and sugar water (SW) containing I3A showed increased I3A levels in fecal material, the liver and serum compared to mice given the same WD and SW without I3A (Figure 1A, B, and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice that were given WD and sugar water (SW) containing I3A showed increased I3A levels in serum compared to mice given the same WD and SW without I3A.
source: Mice that were given WD and sugar water (SW) containing I3A showed increased I3A levels in fecal material, the liver and serum compared to mice given the same WD and SW without I3A (Figure 1A, B, and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WD-fed mice had elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels compared to control mice, indicating liver injury.
source: Compared to CN, WD-fed mice had elevated serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, indicating liver injury.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, and the interpretation that elevated ALT indicates liver injury is based on established knowledge.

claim: Treatment of WD-fed mice with the high dose of I3A (WD-100) significantly reduced serum ALT levels 2 weeks after beginning the I3A treatment (week 10) and beyond.
source: Treatment of WD-fed mice with the high dose of I3A (WD-100) significantly reduced serum ALT levels 2 weeks after beginning the I3A treatment (week 10, Figure 1D) and beyond.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: I3A treatment reduced liver triglycerides (TG) in a dose-dependent manner at week 16.
source: Additionally, I3A treatment reduced liver triglycerides (TG) in a dose-dependent manner at week 16 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: I3A treatment improved liver steatosis in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Scoring of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained liver sections indicated that the I3A treatment improved liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, and lobular inflammation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by histological scoring data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: I3A treatment improved hepatocyte ballooning in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Scoring of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained liver sections indicated that the I3A treatment improved liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, and lobular inflammation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by histological scoring data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: I3A treatment improved lobular inflammation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Scoring of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained liver sections indicated that the I3A treatment improved liver steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, and lobular inflammation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by histological scoring data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Treatment with I3A didn't alter weight increase compared to WD-fed mice.
source: Treatment with I3A didn't alter weight increase nor food intake compared to WD-fed mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Treatment with I3A didn't alter food intake compared to WD-fed mice.
source: Treatment with I3A didn't alter weight increase nor food intake compared to WD-fed mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: All pro-inflammatory cytokines in the panel (e.g. Tnfa, Il-6, Ccl2) were significantly elevated in livers of WD mice compared to CN.
source: All pro-inflammatory cytokines in the panel (e.g. Tnfa, Il-6, Ccl2) were significantly elevated in livers of WD mice compared to CN (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with I3A reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Treatment with I3A reduced the expression of these cytokines in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WD upregulated IL-10, considered an anti-inflammatory cytokine.
source: Interestingly, WD upregulated IL-10, considered an anti-inflammatory cytokine, and I3A treatment downregulated this cytokine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: I3A treatment downregulated IL-10.
source: Interestingly, WD upregulated IL-10, considered an anti-inflammatory cytokine, and I3A treatment downregulated this cytokine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: I3A, provided via drinking water, attenuates diet-induced hepatic steatosis, cellular injury, and inflammation in mice.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that I3A, provided via drinking water, attenuates diet-induced hepatic steatosis, cellular injury, and inflammation in mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: NAFLD is associated with alterations in liver bile acids in mice and humans.
source: Studies in mice and humans showed that NAFLD is associated with alterations in liver bile acids.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from studies in mice and humans.

claim: The ratio of chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) to cholic acid (CD) greatly decreased when HepG12 and AML12 cells were treated with I3A.
source: Previously, we found that the ratio of chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) to cholic acid (CD) greatly decreased when HepG12 and AML12 cells were treated with I3A, indicating that I3A can directly alter host cell bile acid metabolism in vitro (Krishnan et al., 2018).
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors, supported by citation to Krishnan et al., 2018.

claim: I3A can directly alter host cell bile acid metabolism in vitro.
source: Previously, we found that the ratio of chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) to cholic acid (CD) greatly decreased when HepG12 and AML12 cells were treated with I3A, indicating that I3A can directly alter host cell bile acid metabolism in vitro (Krishnan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the previous finding, supported by citation to Krishnan et al., 2018.

claim: Mice in the WD group showed reduced liver total bile acids compared to CN.
source: In the present study, mice in the WD group showed reduced liver total bile acids and CDCA-derived bile acids compared to CN (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mice in the WD group showed reduced CDCA-derived bile acids compared to CN.
source: In the present study, mice in the WD group showed reduced liver total bile acids and CDCA-derived bile acids compared to CN (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with I3A led to a further decrease in the CDCA-derived bile acids.
source: Treatment with I3A led to a further decrease in the CDCA-derived bile acids, consistent with our previous observation of I3A's effect on hepatocytes in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: WD significantly increased the total concentration of FFAs in the liver by 2.7-fold compared to CN.
source: In the liver, WD significantly increased the total concentration of these FFAs by 2.7-fold compared to CN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with I3A had no significant effect on liver FFA concentration, although the total FFA concentration trended lower in the WD-100 group (36% reduction, p=0.11).
source: Treatment with I3A had no significant effect, although the total FFA concentration trended lower in the WD-100 group (36% reduction, p=0.11, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The total FFA concentrations in serum were similar across all four groups.
source: The total FFA concentrations in serum were similar across all four groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fecal microbiome of WD-fed mice showed reduced α-diversity compared to CN.
source: Fecal microbiome of WD-fed mice showed reduced α-diversity compared to CN, which was not further altered upon I3A treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: I3A treatment did not further alter α-diversity of the fecal microbiome in WD-fed mice.
source: Fecal microbiome of WD-fed mice showed reduced α-diversity compared to CN, which was not further altered upon I3A treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The microbiome compositions of CN and WD-fed mice were significantly different.
source: Similarity analysis using the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity metric showed that the microbiome compositions of CN and WD-fed mice were significantly different (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The fecal microbiome compositions of WD-fed mice did not change significantly upon I3A treatment.
source: The fecal microbiome compositions of WD-fed mice did not change significantly upon I3A treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At week 16, the relative abundance of phylum Verrucomicrobia increased in WD-fed mice.
source: At week 16, the relative abundance of phylum Verrucomicrobia increased, whereas Bacteroidetes decreased.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At week 16, the relative abundance of phylum Bacteroidetes decreased in WD-fed mice.
source: At week 16, the relative abundance of phylum Verrucomicrobia increased, whereas Bacteroidetes decreased.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) detected 18 taxa showing significant differences in relative abundance between the WD group and CN, including an expansion of the genus Akkermansia and reduction of family Muribaculaceae.
source: Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) detected 18 taxa showing significant differences in relative abundance between the WD group and CN, including an expansion of the genus Akkermansia and reduction of family Muribaculaceae.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Only three genera showed significant shifts in WD-fed mice upon I3A treatment.
source: In contrast, only three genera showed significant shifts in WD-fed mice upon I3A treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The fecal metabolome of WD-fed mice was significantly different from CN.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of untargeted LC-MS data showed that the fecal metabolome of WD-fed mice was significantly different from CN, whereas the metabolomes of WD-100 and WD groups largely overlapped (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The metabolomes of WD-100 and WD groups largely overlapped.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of untargeted LC-MS data showed that the fecal metabolome of WD-fed mice was significantly different from CN, whereas the metabolomes of WD-100 and WD groups largely overlapped (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Treatment with I3A had minimal effects on the fecal microbiota composition and metabolome of WD-fed mice.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that treatment with I3A had minimal effects on the fecal microbiota composition and metabolome of WD-fed mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the metagenomic and metabolomic data presented in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The liver metabolome of WD-fed mice was significantly different from CN.
source: Projections of all annotated features onto latent variables from PLS-DA showed that the liver metabolome of WD-fed mice was significantly different from CN (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The low dose I3A (WD-50) group completely overlapped with the WD group in liver metabolome.
source: The low dose I3A (WD-50) group completely overlapped with the WD group, whereas the high dose (WD-100) group was significantly different from both WD and CN groups (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The high dose (WD-100) group was significantly different from both WD and CN groups in liver metabolome.
source: The low dose I3A (WD-50) group completely overlapped with the WD group, whereas the high dose (WD-100) group was significantly different from both WD and CN groups (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism was significantly altered by WD and reversed by the high-dose I3A treatment.
source: Enrichment analysis based on KEGG pathways (Figure 3C) showed that nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism and steroid hormone biosynthesis were significantly altered by WD (CN vs WD), which were reversed by the high-dose I3A treatment (WD vs WD-100).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data and pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Steroid hormone biosynthesis was significantly altered by WD and reversed by the high-dose I3A treatment.
source: Enrichment analysis based on KEGG pathways (Figure 3C) showed that nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism and steroid hormone biosynthesis were significantly altered by WD (CN vs WD), which were reversed by the high-dose I3A treatment (WD vs WD-100).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data and pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The high dose of I3A restored WD-induced depletion of metabolites in the upper kynurenine branch.
source: The high dose of I3A restored WD-induced depletion of metabolites in the upper kynurenine branch, and ameliorated WD-induced increases in niacin and nicotinamide in the lower branch.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The high dose of I3A ameliorated WD-induced increases in niacin and nicotinamide in the lower branch of tryptophan metabolism.
source: The high dose of I3A restored WD-induced depletion of metabolites in the upper kynurenine branch, and ameliorated WD-induced increases in niacin and nicotinamide in the lower branch.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The effects of I3A on tryptophan metabolites were dose-dependent.
source: These effects were dose-dependent, as they were not present in the WD-50 group.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mice in the WD group showed elevated levels of long-chain 3-hydroxylacyl-carnitines compared to CN.
source: Compared to CN, mice in the WD group showed elevated levels of long-chain 3-hydroxylacyl-carnitines.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Long-chain 3-hydroxylacyl-carnitines are closely linked to 3-hydroxylacyl-CoAs, which are intermediates of beta-oxidation.
source: These acyl-carnitines are closely linked to 3-hydroxylacyl-CoAs, which are intermediates of beta-oxidation, and their accumulations suggest incomplete beta-oxidation (Su et al., 2005; Natarajan and Ibdah, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Su et al., 2005 and Natarajan and Ibdah, 2018.

claim: Accumulation of long-chain 3-hydroxylacyl-carnitines suggests incomplete beta-oxidation.
source: These acyl-carnitines are closely linked to 3-hydroxylacyl-CoAs, which are intermediates of beta-oxidation, and their accumulations suggest incomplete beta-oxidation (Su et al., 2005; Natarajan and Ibdah, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Su et al., 2005 and Natarajan and Ibdah, 2018.

claim: Treatment with the high dose of I3A significantly reversed accumulations of long-chain 3-hydroxylacyl-carnitines.
source: Treatment with the high dose of I3A significantly reversed these accumulations.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The effect of I3A on acyl-carnitines was dose-dependent.
source: As was the case for tryptophan metabolites, the effect of I3A on acyl-carnitines was dose-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The WD group had a protein abundance profile significantly different from CN.
source: Latent variable projections from PLS-DA on liver proteomics data (Figure 4A) showed that the WD group had a protein abundance profile significantly different from CN (p<10–6, Hotelling's T2).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The effect of I3A on liver proteome was dose-dependent.
source: The effect of I3A was dose-dependent; whereas the WD-50 group was not significantly different from the WD group, the WD-100 group was significantly different from the WD group (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The WD-50 group was not significantly different from the WD group in liver proteome.
source: The effect of I3A was dose-dependent; whereas the WD-50 group was not significantly different from the WD group, the WD-100 group was significantly different from the WD group (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The WD-100 group was significantly different from the WD group in liver proteome (p<0.001).
source: The effect of I3A was dose-dependent; whereas the WD-50 group was not significantly different from the WD group, the WD-100 group was significantly different from the WD group (p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The PLS-DA projections for WD-100 were closer to CN than WD, but still significantly different from CN.
source: The PLS-DA projections for WD-100 were closer to CN than WD, but still significantly different from CN.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The I3A treatment partially reversed the diet-induced alterations in the liver proteome in a dose-dependent manner.
source: These results suggest that the I3A treatment partially reversed the diet-induced alterations in the liver proteome in a dose-dependent manner, similar to the trend observed for the liver metabolome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the proteomics data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids was a metabolic pathway common to both sets of enriched pathways (CN vs WD and WD-100 vs WD).
source: One metabolic pathway, biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids, was common to both sets of enriched pathways.
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Platelet glycoprotein 4 (CD36), a major fatty acid uptake protein, was elevated in the WD group compared to CN.
source: Platelet glycoprotein 4 (CD36), a major fatty acid uptake protein, was elevated in the WD group compared to CN.
evidence: This is supported by targeted proteomics data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The abundance of CD36 was decreased, but not significantly, in the WD-100 group compared to WD.
source: The abundance of CD36 was decreased, but not significantly, in the WD-100 group compared to WD (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by targeted proteomics data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The abundance of fatty acid synthase (Fasn) was not significantly different between the WD group and CN.
source: The abundance of fatty acid synthase (Fasn) was not significantly different between the WD group and CN but was decreased in the WD-100 group compared to the WD group (Figure 5A).
